```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_dagitty <- requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(pollinatoR)
```

A cage trial randomises the arm, so the contrast between caged and open plants
is causal by design. Three questions are not settled by the randomisation.
Which covariates may enter the model without changing what the contrast means?
What does the cage itself do to the plants? And when the question turns from
the treatment to the insects (which visitors drive the contribution), what
protects a comparison between fields that were never randomised? This vignette
works through each on one simulated field study.

## The study

Thirty canola fields, six caged and six open plants in each. Pod count is the
response. Vegetative weight is recorded at harvest, and bee visits are counted
per plant. Fertility varies between fields and is not recorded: it raises pod
count and attracts more bees.

```{r data}
set.seed(47)
n_field <- 30L
fields <- sprintf("F%02d", seq_len(n_field))
fertility <- setNames(rnorm(n_field, 0, 0.25), fields)
study <- expand.grid(
  plant = seq_len(6L),
  trt = c("Caged", "Open"),
  field = fields,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
f <- fertility[study$field]
open <- study$trt == "Open"
study$bees <- rpois(n_field, exp(1.8 + 1.2 * fertility))[match(study$field, fields)] +
  rpois(nrow(study), 1)
study$veg <- round(rgamma(nrow(study), shape = 15, rate = 15 / (40 * exp(0.25 * open))), 1)
study$pods <- rnbinom(
  nrow(study),
  mu = exp(4 + f + 0.15 * open + 0.012 * study$veg),
  size = 20
)
head(study)
```

Pollinator access was planted to raise vegetative weight by about 28%, and
vegetative weight raises pod count. Access also raises pod count directly.
The loss share without pollinators is about 0.25 in total, of which the direct
part, with vegetative weight held fixed, is $1 - e^{-0.15} = 0.14$.

## A graph for the study

The graph states what causes what. Vegetative weight weighed at harvest is
downstream of the arm: access changes how the plant grows. That is the reading
the data were simulated under, and it is the reading supported where it has
been tested: in Zou et al. (2017), closed-cage canola carried more straw
biomass than plants in open-top cages.

```{r graph, eval = has_dagitty}
pd <- pollin_data(
  study,
  "pods",
  "trt",
  unit = "field",
  adjust = "veg",
  exposures = "bees"
)
ds <- pollin_design(pd, c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"), "multi_site")
g_harvest <- pollin_dag(
  ds,
  "dag {
    trt -> veg -> yield
    trt -> yield
    fertility -> bees -> yield
    fertility -> yield
    fertility [latent]
  }",
  "yield"
)
g_harvest
```

The graph gives the adjustment set for the total effect of the arm (none is
needed, since the arm was randomised) and for the direct effect (vegetative
weight). It classes vegetative weight as a mediator of the arm. It also says
that the effect of bees on pod count has no adjustment set: fertility is
latent, and it opens a path from bees to yield that nothing recorded can close.

## Total and direct effects

Adjusting for a mediator is not a precision choice. It changes the question
from "what does pollinator access do" to "what does access do apart from its
effect on vegetative weight". With the graph, the package refuses the first
estimand while vegetative weight sits in `adjust`:

```{r guard, eval = has_dagitty, error = TRUE}
pollin_guard_posttreatment(ds, dag = g_harvest)
```

The total effect is fitted from data that do not adjust for it. The direct
effect is asked for by name, with the mediator held fixed, and every table it
produces says so.

```{r effects}
pd_total <- pollin_data(study, "pods", "trt", unit = "field", exposures = "bees")
ds_total <- pollin_design(pd_total, c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"), "multi_site")
est_total <- pollin_estimand(ds_total, "dependence", "ratio", "loss")

pd_veg <- pollin_data(study, "pods", "trt", unit = "field", adjust = "veg")
ds_veg <- pollin_design(pd_veg, c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"), "multi_site")
est_direct <- pollin_estimand(
  ds_veg,
  "dependence",
  "ratio",
  "loss",
  effect = "direct",
  mediators = "veg"
)

fit_total <- pollin_fit(est_total)
fit_direct <- pollin_fit(est_direct)
pollin_effects(fit_total)
pollin_effects(fit_direct)
```

The two numbers answer different questions, and only the first is what the
crop would lose without pollinators. `pollin_value()` therefore values the
total effect and refuses the direct one:

```{r value, error = TRUE}
canola <- pollin_market(
  quantity = 3600,
  price = 700,
  unit = "t",
  currency = "AUD",
  year = 2025,
  source = "Illustrative inputs"
)
pollin_value(pollin_draws(fit_direct, n = 1000L, seed = 1L), canola,
             channel = "dependence")
```

If vegetative weight were measured before flowering, the arm could not have
changed it. The graph then has no edge from `trt` to `veg`, vegetative weight
is pre-treatment, and the estimand builds with it declared. The effect stays a
total effect, and the fit of a total effect takes no covariates:

```{r preflowering, eval = has_dagitty}
g_pre <- pollin_dag(
  ds,
  "dag { trt -> yield; veg -> yield; fertility -> bees -> yield; fertility -> yield; fertility [latent] }",
  "yield"
)
pollin_estimand(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss", dag = g_pre)
```

Which branch holds is a fact about the protocol, not about the data, and the
graph is where it is written down.

## The cage itself

A closed cage shades and shelters the plant as well as keeping insects out.
The loss share above compares caged with uncaged plants, so it includes any
effect of the cage on pod count. Two remedies exist.

With a sham arm, a device identical to the cage that lets insects in, the
dependence can be read against the sham (`reference = "sham"`) and the cage
effect itself is estimated by the `cage` family; *A three-arm exclusion trial*
shows both.

Without one, the share can be bounded. If the cage multiplies pod count
without pollinators by a factor `k`, the share net of the cage is
`1 - (1 - D) / k`. `pollin_bound()` takes a range for `k` and reports the
bounds per draw:

```{r bound}
pollin_bound(pollin_draws(fit_total, n = 2000L, seed = 1L), cage_factor = c(1, 1.2))
```

The range has no default. It has to come from evidence about the device, such
as a sham arm in another trial of the same crop.

## Which visitors drive the contribution

The moderation of the contribution by bee visits compares fields, and fields
were not randomised to their bees. `pollin_moderation()` splits the exposure
into a within-field and a between-field part and reports the bees' slope among
the caged plants, which insects could not reach:

```{r moderation}
m <- pollin_moderation(ds_total, "pods")
m
```

Neither moderation term differs from zero here. The negative control does: in
the caged arm, pod count rises with the field's bee count, which cannot be
pollination. It is the fertility that brings both, and the graph above already
said that the effect of bees is not identified in this study. Given the graph,
`pollin_moderation(ds, "pods", dag = g_harvest)` refuses for that reason.

The negative control detects a field variable that raises both arms alike. It
cannot detect one that changes the contrast itself, and the assumption table
of the moderation result says so.

## Whole yield and its components

A dependence estimated on one yield component is not the dependence of yield.
Seed yield per plant is the product of pods per plant, seeds per pod and seed
weight, and a plant that sets fewer seeds can fill them better. Suppose the
study also weighed the seeds of each plant and counted seeds per pod, and
that seeds per pod respond strongly to pollinator access while seed weight
compensates:

```{r components}
set.seed(48)
study$seeds <- rgamma(nrow(study), shape = 20, rate = 20 / exp(2.5 + 0.35 * open))
study$weight <- rgamma(nrow(study), shape = 30, rate = 30 / exp(1.2 - 0.12 * open))
study$yield <- study$pods * study$seeds * study$weight / 1000
pd_yield <- pollin_data(study, c("yield", "pods", "seeds", "weight"), "trt",
  unit = "field")
ds_yield <- pollin_design(pd_yield, c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"), "rcbd")
fit_yield <- pollin_fit(
  pollin_estimand(ds_yield, "dependence", "ratio", "loss"),
  family = list(
    yield = stats::Gamma(link = "log"), pods = glmmTMB::nbinom2(),
    seeds = stats::Gamma(link = "log"), weight = stats::Gamma(link = "log")
  )
)
pollin_decompose(fit_yield, "yield", c("pods", "seeds", "weight"),
  n_boot = 100L, seed = 1L)
```

On the log scale the effect on yield is the sum of the effects on the
components plus an interaction term, which is near zero here because the
components vary independently within each arm. The shares say how much of the
yield effect each component carries. Seed weight carries a negative share and
is flagged as compensating. A loss share computed from any single component
misstates the dependence of yield: seeds per pod alone would understate it
here, and seed weight alone would give it the wrong sign. The intervals come from resampling whole fields
and refitting all four models on each resample; 100 replicates keep this
vignette quick, and an analysis would use about 2,000.

## Sensitivity

For the total effect on a count, the E-value states how strongly an unmeasured
confounder would have to be associated with both the arm and the response to
explain the contrast away:

```{r evalue}
pollin_sensitivity(pollin_effects(fit_total))
```

In a randomised trial this guards against a failure of the randomisation
rather than against ordinary confounding. The package forms no E-value for a
direct effect, a difference or a continuous response, and for a moderation
term it reports the link-scale bias that would move the term to zero.

## Reference

Zou, Y., Xiao, H., Bianchi, F. J. J. A., Jauker, F., Luo, S., & van der Werf,
W. (2017). Wild pollinators enhance oilseed rape yield in small-holder farming
systems in China. *BMC Ecology*, *17*, 6.
https://doi.org/10.1186/s12898-017-0116-1
